ambivalent about trade barriers as an economic policy. On one hand I think </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8366cf8d-937b-4102-882c-51b9ab3db5cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">targeted tariffs</a><span> and other trade barriers can be used to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/00ff8c8d-8b4e-4d65-a0cf-1549dcd8329a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">protect strategic industries</a><span> from surges in underpriced import competition, especially by geopolitical rivals. On the other hand, broad tariffs like the ones Trump has used </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65766e0a-6f90-44f9-a4db-a3e0549c4638?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">are generally bad</a><span> — they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed681be3-6f02-4c7f-80aa-0db2d014fee5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">hurt domestic manufacturing</a><span> by making intermediate goods more expensive, they limit scale for domestic companies, etc. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And yet I do think that Europe should erect much higher trade barriers — both tariffs and non-tariff barriers — against Chinese high-tech manufactured export goods. The basic reason is that it’s important to protect Europe’s nascent modern defense industry. But I also think that blocking Chinese exports might nudge China to change its economic model to one that benefits regular Chinese people more. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In other words, China-Europe trade has some unusual characteristics right now that make trade barriers a much smarter idea than usual. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, let’s talk about what’s going on with the Chinese economy. For the past few years, China’s government has unleashed an unprecedented torrent of subsidies for high-tech manufacturing industries. This — along with structural factors about how the Chinese economy works — has resulted in China making big global market share gains in industries like autos, pharmaceuticals, and shipbuilding. No one knows just how much of China’s market share gains are a result of government support, but as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f71022f0-a57e-4836-a18c-4c79a33f39d6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Paul Hannon reports</a><span>, the OECD estimates that it’s more than half:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Government subsidies have driven most of the increase in the global market share of Chinese businesses over the past two decades as they have received three to eight times more support than their competitors, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said Monday…The analysis is based on the OECD’s Manufacturing Groups and Industrial Corporations database, which includes subsidy estimates and financial information for 525 of the world’s largest manufacturing groups spread across 15 key industrial sectors…[T]he OECD database tracks the amounts that firms are actually given…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Industrial firms based in China receive more subsidies than their competitors based everywhere else,” the OECD said…For Chinese businesses, however, the share of [market share] gains explained by subsidies was…60%.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Rhodium Group has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3004c302-b895-4987-b783-ac77834de659?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a deeper dive</a><span> into China’s new industrial policy. Essentially, instead of selecting a few industries to specialize in, China’s leaders just want the country to dominate </span><em>everything</em><span> — not just manufacturing, but services as well:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China’s industrial strategy…</span><strong>is becoming more systemic and pervasive,</strong><span> extending across all layers of production, from upstream inputs and industrial equipment to downstream applications, services, and frontier technologies…China’s next-generation industrial policy represents a shift from targeted sectoral intervention to what can be described as an “industrial policy of everything.”…While [Made in China 2025] focused on a defined set of strategic emerging industries, current policy frameworks extend across mature sectors, foundational supply chain nodes, and frontier technologies alike…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even in mature industries facing overcapacity and severe price pressures, </span><strong>Beijing</strong><span> </span><strong>is providing continued support and pushing firms to upgrade production technologies to gain market share and lower production costs, rather than cutting capacity</strong><span>…</span><strong>Services, relatively neglected in earlier rounds of industrial policy, are getting more attention</strong><span>[.]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, China does not want</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> to exist in a trading system, where goods are traded for other goods. China wants to make all the goods, and have other countries pay for those goods with debt. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two basic reasons China is doing this. The first is pure </span><em>mercantilism</em><span>; China is trying to export its way out of the economic slump created by its housing bust. The second, as the Rhodium Group report explains, is </span><em>power</em><span>. If China controls key segments of other countries’ supply chains, it can use the threat of export controls to bring those countries to heel. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What should other countries do about this? The U.S. has chosen to respond with tariffs. These are of limited effectiveness, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e741e335-4cf5-4807-8ad9-7d358a4283f8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The question is now what Europe and other developed countries — who have marginally more rational decision-making processes — are going to do about China’s attempt to dominate all tradable industries. One proposal — which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dd945fcf-1e51-48d7-aa52-5622c55d36e9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Germany seems to be following</a><span> so far — is to do </span><em>nothing</em><span>, and to simply let China make all the physical objects in the world, while focusing on services instead. This is essentially </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c7c5ac49-15eb-4442-98f3-d4460f8af1e9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the proposal of Tej Parikh</a><span>, who writes that China “has a comparative advantage in industrial policy itself”, and that trying to compete with China in any manufacturing industry is therefore doomed to fail. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This annoys me, because it represents a deep misunderstanding of the entire concept of comparative advantage! The theory of comparative advantage is about </span><em>traded goods</em><span>; it’s about which traded goods can be produced relatively more cheaply by which countries. If I’m better at making TVs than cars, and you’re better at making cars than TVs, then I’ll make TVs and you’ll make cars and then we’ll trade. That’s how comparative advantage works.  This is why you cannot have a “comparative advantage in industrial policy”. Industrial policy is a </span><em>production input</em><span>, not a traded good. No one buys and sells industrial policy! </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“OK, Noah,” you’re about to say. “Stop being a pedant. You know what he means. He means China is better at making anything and everything, because they use industrial policy for everything.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yes, I know that’s what he means. And yes, this reflects a deep misunderstanding of the concept of comparative advantage.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> Even if one country is better at making everything, it doesn’t have a </span><em>comparative advantage</em><span> in everything. That’s impossible. Every country has a comparative advantage at something!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s why in the theory of comparative advantage, </span><em>trade is balanced.</em><span> In the real world, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/057e1e6f-c279-41b1-9597-478f0be7b9b0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">China’s massive trade surplus</a><span> means that trade is not balanced; much of the time, China isn’t trading goods for other goods, </span><em>it’s trading goods for IOUs</em><span>. That kind of unbalanced trade is something that just doesn’t happen in the theory of comparative advantage. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OK, so that was a bit of a rant. The real point here is that Parikh’s preferred solution — that every country except China should focus on innovation, and leave the making of everything to the Chinese — is simply ridiculous. First of all, it doesn’t deal at all with the issue of supply chain vulnerabilities. Second of all, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/67968bcf-5c42-4930-84b3-4886076391d3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">China has an industrial policy for innovation</a><span>, too — in fact, it’s China’s most important industrial policy. The idea of “We’ll do the innovation while China makes everything” sounds straight out of 2002 — and it was obviously wrong even back then. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cold, hard fact is that Europe needs to do </span><em>something</em><span>, or risk losing its sovereignty to foreign conquerors. China — the very country that Europe’s free-traders are now suggesting should supply every single manufactured good — is </span><em>waging a proxy war against Europe</em><span> even as we speak. China </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ba8c12c-3fb9-4294-b16f-1348faf398ca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">trains Russian soldiers</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/728780a3-2e08-4399-a0d1-2eab3cf0c4d1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">provides Russia with battlefield intelligence</a><span> in its war against Ukraine, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef0fcec4-1d17-406a-886a-2509a200c1d4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">helps out Russian defense manufacturers</a><span>, and even </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/01d26a4f-2fb2-4b49-a575-e7fdf25e256b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">does some defense manufacturing</a><span> for Russia — in addition to buying Russian oil and keeping the Russian economy afloat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And this is all while Russia is </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/85371373-bc18-4a05-8ec6-ef0d005e6a68?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">actively threatening to invade the EU</a></em><span>. If Russia eventually does invade, Europe will need to make </span><em>large amounts of drones</em><span> to resist the invasion. All militaries that are not centered around large masses of drones are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/63fb2628-9a06-4c05-bbbe-25fae36635e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">now obsolete</a><span> — when NATO conducts war games against drone-equipped Ukrainian units, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfc078ec-4b04-4e57-a8bf-2478f5814645?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Ukrainians easily triumph</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But both Europe and Ukraine </span><em>cannot currently make drones from scratch</em><span> without relying on Chinese industry. Many of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/324a7c7b-e9a7-46c1-9283-259d0938e1cf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the components and materials</a><span> that go into making a drone are controlled by China — things like radio modules, lithium-ion batteries, electric motors, navigation cameras, and even carbon frames. Europe cannot currently make these — or can’t make many of them, at least.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If Russia were to invade Europe, China could simply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62c3c950-b358-4263-84b5-bf659ce833ff?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">decide not to sell Europe the components</a><span> it needs to make drones. Why wouldn’t it? China has already proven itself </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/703474cd-3922-42b9-8146-a6c2f4e11c8d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">perfectly willing</a><span> to use export controls on rare earths and other upstream technologies to throttle other countries’ defense industries. And a Europe cowed and dominated by China’s most important ally would probably be more useful to Xi Jinping than a free and independent Europe that steers its own destiny. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If Russia invaded Europe and China simultaneously halted the export of drone components, Europe would be a lost cause. Unless Europe could assemble upstream industries for drone components from scratch before Russia’s drone-equipped armies marched across the Baltics and into Poland, the war would quickly be lost for lack of weapons. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Whether they realize it yet or not, Europe’s dependence on China for the manufacture of many key defense inputs puts it at China’s mercy. This is a downside to free trade that the folks who advocate a European retreat from manufacturing simply fail to engage with or acknowledge. It provides a strong rationale for putting up trade barriers against the import of certain intermediate goods — something that harms economic efficiency, but is necessary for defense. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When invading armies are burning your country to the ground, you should worry less about deadweight loss than about being dead. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But those who wring their hands about the economic losses should take heart. Blocking the import of Chinese goods might harm economic efficiency, but it could have some positive knock-on effects in terms of </span><em>political economy</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For all China’s high-tech wizardry, its big industrial policy push doesn’t seem to be doing much to </span><em>help the actual people of China</em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The real estate industry, which previously created plenty of labor demand and broad-based wealth for regular Chinese people, is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e026ef54-ecd2-44d7-aaed-e41a0d4686bb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">still in the dumps</a><span> and may even be getting worse. The continued property bust is weighing on aggregate demand — Fixed-asset investment </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/632e3d33-55e5-4d15-937a-8e039232fa54?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">is shrinking</a><span>, while retail sales have flatlined. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Industrial policy for everything” was supposed to fill the hole left by real estate, but it isn’t doing a very good job of it. Because the rise in Chinese manufacturing output is being done mostly for export, regular Chinese people aren’t able to share in the bounty the policies are creating. China’s technology level is advancing, its companies are winning global market share, and it’s gaining control over key strategic technological choke points.
